notes: Reasoning Ability topic package 2 for BATCH_010 (Month and Date-Based Puzzles, Puzzles (Other), Syllogism, Inequality): 43 original questions built by tools/packages/REAS_pkg2.py. Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement or recomputed with datetime; syllogisms checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over every integer ordering (with a wider-range cross-check).

stimuli.title: Five filled and hollow shapes for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, five shapes are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A ◆ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ◇ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A ▼ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ▽ B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A ○ B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ◆ means >, ◇ means ≥, ▼ means <, ▽ means ≤ and ○ means =. Rewrite the statements with ordinary signs, join them into a chain and test each conclusion.

stimuli.title: Five children and their chocolates
stimuli.content:
Five children Golu, Hiya, Jojo, Kiku and Lalli have different numbers of chocolates.

- Hiya has more chocolates than Golu but fewer than Kiku.
- Jojo has fewer chocolates than Golu.
- Lalli has more chocolates than Kiku.
stimuli.solution: Golu < Hiya < Kiku < Lalli, and Jojo < Golu. Order (most first): Lalli, Kiku, Hiya, Golu, Jojo.

stimuli.title: Six school posts and six subjects
stimuli.content:
Six teachers Kamini, Lokesh, Madhav, Naina, Oorja and Pratik of a school hold six different posts. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: Principal, Vice-Principal, Coordinator, Senior Teacher, Teacher and Assistant Teacher. Each teaches a different subject among Maths, Science, English, History, Art and Music.

- The Maths teacher is senior to exactly four of the others.
- The History teacher is the Principal.
- Kamini is junior to the Maths teacher but senior to Pratik.
- Lokesh is the most junior, and he teaches neither Music nor Art.
- Pratik teaches Science, and Naina teaches Music and is junior to Pratik.
- Madhav is senior to Oorja.
- The Art teacher is senior to the Science teacher.
stimuli.solution:
The Maths teacher has four people below: Vice-Principal. The Principal teaches History. Lokesh is the Assistant Teacher (rank 6). Pratik teaches Science and Naina Music, Naina junior to Pratik; Kamini is junior to the Vice-Principal but senior to Pratik. So Kamini > Pratik > Naina > Lokesh fills ranks 3 to 6: Kamini Coordinator, Pratik Senior Teacher, Naina Teacher. Madhav and Oorja take ranks 1 and 2, Madhav senior: Madhav Principal (History), Oorja Vice-Principal (Maths). Lokesh teaches neither Music nor Art, so English; Kamini teaches Art (and is senior to the Science teacher, as required).

Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Assistant Teacher–English.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All robins are finches.
Some wrens are robins.

Conclusions:
I. Some wrens are finches.
II. All finches are wrens.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: The wrens that are robins are also finches, so some wrens are finches (I). Nothing says every finch is a wren (II).
steps: Wren ∩ robin ≠ ∅ and robins ⊂ finches ⇒ I follows
Finches outside wrens are possible ⇒ II not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion II is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only II' are wrong; I holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Some magpies are cuckoos.
Some cuckoos are not orioles.

Conclusions:
I. Some magpies are orioles.
II. All orioles are cuckoos.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Two particular statements give no definite link: the magpies among the cuckoos may all lie in the part that is not orioles, so I is not certain; and orioles may lie outside the cuckoos, so II is not certain.
steps: Some + Some not ⇒ no definite conclusion
I and II both fail in some valid diagram
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails in at least one valid diagram, so 'Only I', 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Statements:

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: H < D ≥ W = K > T ≥ Q

Conclusions:
I. H < K
II. W > Q

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: H < D ≥ W turns at D, so H and K are unrelated (I). W = K > T ≥ Q gives W > Q (II).
steps: I: turn at D ⇒ no relation
II: W = K > T ≥ Q ⇒ W > Q, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

I. E ≥ M
II. J > G

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: E = P ≥ G ≥ M gives E ≥ M (I). J ≥ F > M ≤ G turns at M, so J and G are unrelated (II).
steps: I: E = P ≥ G ≥ M ⇒ E ≥ M, true
II: turn at M ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: L ◆ R, R ○ B, B ▼ H, H ◇ N

Conclusions:
I. L ◆ H
II. N ◆ R

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: L > R = B < H ≥ N. Both conclusions cross the turn at B (R = B < H), so neither is fixed.
steps: Decode: L > R, R = B, B < H, H ≥ N
Chain: L > R = B < H ≥ N
I and II cross the turn at B ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: C ▽ Y, Y ▼ U, U ○ F, F ◆ I

Conclusions:
I. C ▼ I
II. U ◆ C

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: C ≤ Y < U = F > I. C and I are on opposite sides of the turn at U = F, so C < I is not certain (I). U > Y ≥ C gives U > C (II).
steps: Decode: C ≤ Y, Y < U, U = F, F > I
I: turn at F ⇒ no relation
II: U > Y ≥ C ⇒ U > C, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

II: A > O = X ≥ E ⇒ A > E, true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: N ≥ X; X > Q; Q ≤ V; V = H; H < E; A ≤ N

Conclusions:
I. N > Q
II. E > Q
III. E > V

Which of the conclusions is/are definitely true?

options.text: All I, II and III are true
Only I and II are true
Only II and III are true
Only I and III are true

solution.concept: Three conclusions tested against one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: A ≤ N ≥ X > Q ≤ V = H < E. N ≥ X > Q gives N > Q (I); E > H = V ≥ Q gives E > Q (II); E > H = V gives E > V (III). All three are true.
steps: Chain: A ≤ N ≥ X > Q ≤ V = H < E
I: N > Q, true
II: E > Q, true
III: E > V, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other options drops one conclusion that does follow; none of I, II, III crosses the turn at Q.
solution.final_answer: Option A: All I, II and III are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which of the following expressions is 'R > D' definitely true and 'R > K' definitely false?

solution.concept: Two requirements at once: one relation forced, another impossible
solution.explanation: In K ≥ M = R > S ≥ D, R > S ≥ D gives R > D, and K ≥ M = R gives R ≤ K, so R > K can never hold.
steps: Need R > D forced and R ≤ K forced
K ≥ M = R ⇒ R ≤ K; R > S ≥ D ⇒ R > D
solution.why_others_wrong: R > M ≥ D = S ≥ K makes R > K true; in K > M ≤ R > S ≥ D and D < S = R ≥ M ≤ K, R and K are separated by a turn at M, so R > K is possible rather than definitely false.
solution.final_answer: Option B: K ≥ M = R > S ≥ D

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five friends Arpita, Bhola, Chinmay, Dimple and Elvis have their birthdays in five different months from August to December, one in each month.
- Chinmay's birthday is in October.
- Bhola's birthday is in a 30-day month before Chinmay's.
- Dimple's birthday is three months after Arpita's.

Whose birthday is in November?

solution.explanation: Chinmay: October. Bhola: the 30-day month before October in the range is September. Dimple is three months after Arpita: of August, November and December, only August → November works. Elvis takes December. November: Dimple.
steps: Chinmay Oct, Bhola Sep
Arpita Aug ⇒ Dimple Nov
Elvis Dec
solution.why_others_wrong: Elvis is in December, Arpita in August and Bhola in September.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Dimple

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Payal borrowed a library book on 27 January 2027 and returned it 9 days later. On the day Payal returned it, Qasim borrowed the same book and kept it for 12 days.

On which date did Qasim return the book?

solution.concept: Adding days across a month end
solution.explanation: January has 31 days: 27 January + 4 days = 31 January, and 5 more days give 5 February (Payal's return). Qasim: 5 February + 12 days = 17 February.
steps: 27 Jan + 9 = 5 Feb
5 Feb + 12 = 17 Feb
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 February and 18 February are one day off (counting 11 or 13 days for Qasim); 14 February treats January as a 28-day month.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 17 February 2027

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
1 January 2026 is a Thursday, and 2026 is not a leap year. Five friends each guess the next year after 2026 whose calendar is exactly the same as that of 2026 (every date falling on the same day of the week): Kavin says 2032, Leela says 2037, Mehr says 2043 and Nagesh says 2036.

Whose guess is correct?

solution.concept: Odd days: +1 for an ordinary year, +2 after a leap year
solution.explanation: A calendar repeats when 1 January falls on the same weekday and the year is of the same type (ordinary). Moving from one 1 January to the next adds 1 weekday after an ordinary year and 2 after a leap year: 2027 Fri, 2028 Sat (leap), 2029 Mon, 2030 Tue, 2031 Wed, 2032 Thu — but 2032 is a leap year, so its calendar differs after February. 2033 Sat, 2034 Sun, 2035 Mon, 2036 Tue (leap), 2037 Thu, ordinary: 2037 repeats 2026.
steps: 1 Jan weekday: 2027 Fri, 2028 Sat, 2029 Mon, 2030 Tue, 2031 Wed, 2032 Thu (leap ✗)
2033 Sat, 2034 Sun, 2035 Mon, 2036 Tue, 2037 Thu (ordinary ✓)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2032 starts on a Thursday but is a leap year; 2043 also repeats 2026 but is not the next one; 2036 starts on a Tuesday.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Leela (2037)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Four doctors Sunil, Tanu, Varsha and Yusra hold four posts in a hospital. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: Medical Superintendent, Chief Medical Officer, Senior Resident and Junior Resident.
- Varsha is senior to Tanu but junior to Yusra.
- Sunil is not the Medical Superintendent.
- Tanu is not the most junior.

Who is the Senior Resident?

solution.explanation: Yusra > Varsha > Tanu. Tanu is not the most junior, so Sunil is the Junior Resident and Tanu the Senior Resident; Varsha is the CMO and Yusra the Medical Superintendent (Sunil is not).
steps: Yusra > Varsha > Tanu
Tanu not last ⇒ Sunil Junior Resident
Tanu Senior Resident
solution.why_others_wrong: Varsha is the CMO, Sunil the Junior Resident and Yusra the Medical Superintendent.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Tanu

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Asha, Babu, Chand, Dolly, Elan and Fatima each go to a swimming pool on one of six days from Sunday to Friday of the same week, one person per day.
- Chand goes on Tuesday, and Babu on the day after Chand.
- Asha goes on the first of the six days.
- Elan goes on Thursday.
- Fatima goes earlier in the week than Dolly.

Who goes on Friday?

solution.explanation: Asha Sunday, Chand Tuesday, Babu Wednesday, Elan Thursday. Monday and Friday remain; Fatima is earlier than Dolly, so Fatima Monday and Dolly Friday.
steps: Asha Sun, Chand Tue, Babu Wed, Elan Thu
Fatima before Dolly ⇒ Fatima Mon, Dolly Fri
solution.why_others_wrong: Fatima goes on Monday, Elan on Thursday and Babu on Wednesday.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Dolly

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Four boxes P, Q, R and S have different weights. On a balance:
- P and Q together exactly balance R and S together.
- P and R together are heavier than Q and S together.
- P and S together are lighter than Q and R together.

Which box is the heaviest?

solution.concept: Add and subtract the balance relations
solution.explanation: Write P + Q = R + S (1), P + R > Q + S (2), P + S < Q + R (3). (2) − (1): R − Q > Q − R, so R > Q. (1) + (3): 2P + Q + S < 2R + Q + S, so R > P. From (1), R − P = Q − S, and R > P, so Q > S; also R > P and (2) + (1) give P > S. So R is heavier than P, Q and S.
steps: R > P > S (and Q > S) ⇒ R heaviest
solution.why_others_wrong: P and Q are each lighter than R; S is the lightest box.
solution.final_answer: Option D: R
